doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

chapter: Denver youth and University of Denver
title: Dance-gig repertoire and learning tunes
summary: Combo books, charts from Las Vegas and Basie material, and learning tunes of the day for dance jobs.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: It sure was but it’s wonderful that we didn’t think it was crazy at that time. I mean we might have sort of complained about it but still there’s nothing like that feeling I guess. Can you remember what your repertoire would have consisted of for those gigs? This would have been around when?

It would be in the latter 60s. Well no, it could be early, in high school I was there in 1960. So yeah the repertoire we played out of the “Combo Ork” Books I think they were called. And the instrumentation worked on about — for about any number of players that you had. And then there were some — I can’t remember the publishers you know. But there wasn’t a lot of music for us to play. In fact by the time I got to college you know you had to, if you wanted to be competitive in these contests that we went to, or the festivals, you know you had to have some good charts. And luckily our director knew some people in Las Vegas and they would supply us with some charts, some good stuff you know, and some Basie things too. And so that’s how we got our repertoire there. But just as far as high school stuff, just buying things off the shelf I mean I think bands are still playing some of that music you know.
Yes. In those times it was AM radio played almost anything you could imagine, but what would the group have done if someone came up, put twenty bucks in the tip jar and said,
“Play some Sinatra”? And if you didn’t know any did you have the wherewithal that you could fake it?

Yeah we probably could — not all of us you know but I mean a quartet could, could play the tunes. Because that was one of the things we did was to start learning tunes and we played combo gigs, you know, with maybe just one horn and a rhythm section, or sometimes two horns, but mainly just one. And you know we called them dance gigs, and so it was mainly just learning tunes, the tunes of the day, Broadway tunes, standards, and having that repertoire of things to do, you know, things to play.
